content: The GRADE system evaluates the quality of evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low. It also considers the balance of benefits and harms at both individual and population levels, patient and healthcare worker values and preferences, resource use, equity, cost-effectiveness, and feasibility across various settings, including resource-limited environments with restricted access to laboratory infrastructure and specialized tests. There is no evidence available regarding the benefits and harms of treatment for drug-resistant leprosy. Consequently, recommendations for this topic are based on expert opinion. The process also identified key research gaps to guide future research agendas for leprosy. These guidelines do not address the programmatic aspects of leprosy management, which are covered by the WHO Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020, titled Accelerating towards a leprosy-free world, along with its accompanying Operational Manual and Monitoring and Evaluation Guide. The diagnosis of leprosy remains reliant on the identification of at least one of three cardinal signs: (i) definite loss of sensation in a pale (hypopigmented) or reddish skin patch; (ii) thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with loss of sensation and/or muscle weakness in the area supplied by that nerve; or (iii) the presence of acid-fast bacilli in a slit-skin smear. No additional diagnostic tests are recommended beyond these standard methods. Diagnosing early leprosy and paucibacillary (PB) leprosy can be challenging. Various serological and laboratory assays have been developed to supplement clinical diagnostic methods. However, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) and lateral flow assays have low diagnostic accuracy for PB leprosy. While some polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based assays demonstrate higher diagnostic accuracy, they lack standardization, are not commercially available, and are difficult to implement in most primary healthcare settings. The guidelines do not recommend any diagnostic tests for asymptomatic contacts of leprosy patients. The predictive accuracy of diagnostic tests for identifying individuals who will develop leprosy is low, with poor positive predictive values. For the treatment of leprosy, the guidelines recommend a three-drug regimen consisting of rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine for all patients. The treatment duration is six months for PB leprosy and 12 months for multibacillary (MB) leprosy. This represents a change from the previous standard treatment for PB leprosy, which involved rifampicin and dapsone for six months. Evidence suggests better clinical outcomes with the three-drug regimen compared to the two-drug regimen. Using the same blister pack for both PB and MB leprosy reduces the risk of misclassification and ensures all patients receive the three-drug regimen. For MB leprosy, the current standard treatment is a three-drug regimen for 12 months. Evidence on the potential benefits and harms of a shorter (six-month) three-drug regimen is limited and inconclusive, with a potential increase in relapse risk. Therefore, the guideline development group (GDG) determined that there is insufficient evidence to recommend shortening the treatment duration for MB leprosy. For rifampicin-resistant leprosy, the guidelines recommend treatment with at least two second-line drugs (clarithromycin, minocycline, or a quinolone) plus clofazimine daily for six months, followed by clofazimine and one of these drugs for an additional 18 months. If ofloxacin resistance is also present, a fluoroquinolone should not be used as part of the second-line treatment. In such cases, the preferred regimen includes six months of clarithromycin, minocycline, and clofazimine, followed by clarithromycin or minocycline plus clofazimine for an additional 18 months. Resistance has been reported in several countries, although the number of affected patients is small. There is no evidence on the benefits and harms of alternative regimens for drug-resistant leprosy, so recommendations are based on expert opinion and the known activity of alternative drugs, including the likelihood of cross-resistance. For the prevention of leprosy, the guidelines recommend the use of single-dose rifampicin (SDR) as preventive treatment for adult and child contacts (aged two years and above) of leprosy patients, after excluding leprosy and tuberculosis (TB) and in the absence of other contraindications. The COLEP randomized controlled trial (RCT) found that SDR in leprosy contacts was associated with a 57% reduction in leprosy risk after two years and a 30% reduction after five to six years. SDR also appears to be highly cost-effective, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of USD 158 per additional prevented leprosy case. The successful implementation of SDR requires programmes to adequately identify and manage contacts of leprosy patients. Given the high stigma associated with leprosy, caution must be exercised when implementing SDR, particularly for contacts outside the patient’s family. Programmes must respect the patient’s decision to disclose or not disclose their diagnosis. If patients do not authorize disclosure, the GDG does not recommend identifying or screening contacts, as this is a prerequisite for prescribing preventive treatment. Treating all community members without identifying contacts may be more feasible and reduce potential harms related to the disclosure of a leprosy diagnosis. Leprosy predominantly affects the skin and peripheral nerves, leading to neuropathy and long-term consequences such as deformities and disability. While leprosy was historically widespread, it is now mainly confined to tropical and subtropical regions. The disease is associated with stigma, particularly when deformities are present. Transmission is poorly understood but is thought to occur through inhalation of droplets containing Mycobacterium leprae (M. leprae). Skin contact or other means of transmission cannot be entirely excluded. Leprosy has a reservoir in armadillos and a few other animals. Up to 95% of individuals exposed to M. leprae do not develop the disease, suggesting that host immunity plays a significant role in disease progression and control. The incubation period is variable, ranging from two to 20 years or longer. The fight against leprosy has achieved significant success, as evidenced by the elimination of leprosy as a public health problem (defined as a point prevalence below 1 per 10,000 population) globally in 2000 and at the national level in most countries by 2005. However, the number of new leprosy cases diagnosed remains significant, with more than 200,000 cases reported in 2016. The new case detection rate, a proxy for the incidence rate, is only slowly declining. Leprosy is diagnosed by identifying at least one of the following cardinal signs: (1) definite loss of sensation in a pale (hypopigmented) or reddish skin patch; (2) thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with loss of sensation and/or muscle weakness in the area supplied by that nerve; or (3) the presence of acid-fast bacilli in a slit-skin smear. Leprosy is a highly variable disease, affecting individuals differently based on their immune response. Patients with a high level of immunity harbor a low number of bacilli and are classified as having PB leprosy. Those with many bacilli in the body are classified as having MB leprosy. In 2016, WHO launched the Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020, Accelerating towards a leprosy-free world, and in 2017, revised the case definitions of PB and MB leprosy. Early diagnosis and complete treatment with multidrug therapy (MDT) remain the key strategies for reducing the disease burden of leprosy. Additionally, the BCG vaccine is an effective tool for leprosy prevention. Standard MDT regimens for PB (two drugs) and MB (three drugs) leprosy were introduced in 1982, with treatment durations of six months for PB leprosy and initially a minimum of 24 months for MB leprosy, later reduced to 12 months in 1998 based on WHO recommendations. MDT is provided in blister packs, each containing four weeks of treatment, with specific packs available for MB and PB leprosy and different doses for adults and children. MDT is provided free of charge globally through an agreement between a pharmaceutical company and WHO. WHO manages the distribution of MDT to countries in coordination with national leprosy programmes. To date, no WHO recommendations on preventive strategies have been issued, although research on different antibiotics and combinations of antibiotics has been conducted since the 1990s.
